Predicting Titanic Passenger Survival

Author

Tahir Hussain, Jaylon Huang, Rakshit Kapoor, and Teeba Obaid

1 Introduction

The sinking of the RMS Titanic on April 15, 1912 remains one of the best-documented maritime disasters in modern history. Historical and sociological studies have shown that survival was strongly shaped by evacuation norms (“women and children first”) and differences in social class (Hall 1986; Elinder and Erixson 2012).

In this project, we ask a predictive research question: how accurately can a passenger’s survival on the Titanic be predicted from demographic and ticket information available prior to departure, and does adding domain-informed optional features and interactions improve upon our core correlation-selected predictors? Using the Kaggle Titanic dataset (Cukierski 2012), we first conduct an exploratory data analysis (EDA) on the 891 labelled training passengers and save the cleaned datasets to data/processed/. We then build and evaluate a regularized logistic regression classification pipeline using 5-fold stratified cross-validation.

2 Exploratory data analysis

This section explores the Titanic passenger data before any model is built. We check the structure of the data and how much of it is missing, compare every passenger characteristic with the outcome we want to predict (whether the passenger survived, coded 1, or died, coded 0), and clean and transform the data so that it is ready for modelling. We finish by ranking the features by how strongly they relate to survival and choosing the four to five that we will carry into the model.

We use Python with pandas (McKinney 2010), scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al. 2011), matplotlib (Hunter 2007) and seaborn (Waskom 2021). The passenger records come from the Kaggle “Titanic: Machine Learning from Disaster” competition (Cukierski 2012). Each row is one passenger. Kaggle supplies two files: a training file of 891 passengers whose survival outcome is known, and a test file of 418 passengers whose outcome is hidden.

2.1 Training and test data

The raw folder holds two files, and we use them exactly as supplied. The training file (train.csv) has 891 passengers with a known outcome, and the test file (test.csv) has 418 passengers whose outcome is hidden. To respect the golden rule of machine learning, every pattern, plot, fill-in value and correlation below is learned from the training file only. The test file is used for two things: counting its missing values, and applying the same cleaning steps that were learned from the training data. Nothing in it influences a decision.

2.2 The variables

Table 1 describes each column in the data. The last column of the table says what we expect to do with it, which we justify in the sections below.

Column in the data Meaning Plan
Survived Outcome: 1 if the passenger survived, 0 if not (the target) Target
Pclass Ticket class: 1 (first), 2 (second) or 3 (third) Candidate
Sex Male or female Candidate
Age Age in years (fractional for infants) Candidate, needs imputation
SibSp Number of siblings or spouses travelling with the passenger Used to build family size
Parch Number of parents or children travelling with the passenger Used to build family size
Fare Ticket price in pounds Candidate, log transform
Cabin Cabin number, mostly missing Reduced to a cabin-recorded flag
Embarked Port of boarding: Cherbourg, Queenstown or Southampton Candidate, needs imputation
Name Passenger name including title (for example Mr or Mrs) Only the title is used
Ticket Ticket number Excluded
PassengerId Row identifier Excluded (identifier only)

The training data has 891 passengers and 12 columns. Passenger class, sex, siblings and spouses, parents and children, and fare are recorded for everyone. Age, cabin and port of boarding have gaps, which we examine next.

Before comparing features, we check how balanced the target is. A model that predicts “did not survive” for everyone would already be right about 62% of the time on this data, so any model we build has to beat that baseline.

Missing values are not always random, so we check whether being missing is itself related to survival.

Code 
overall = train["Survived"].mean()

def rate_bar(ax, data, col, order=None, xlabel="", labels=None):
    """Bar chart of the survival rate for each level of `col`, with group sizes."""
    g = data.groupby(col, observed=True)["Survived"].agg(["mean", "size"])
    if order is not None:
        g = g.reindex(order)
    names = labels if labels is not None else [str(i) for i in g.index]
    bars = ax.bar(names, g["mean"] * 100, color=SURV)
    for b, m, n in zip(bars, g["mean"], g["size"]):
        ax.text(b.get_x() + b.get_width() / 2, m * 100 + 1.5, f"{m:.0%}\n(n={n})",
                ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9)
    ax.axhline(overall * 100, ls="--", color="grey", lw=1, label="Overall survival rate (38%)")
    ax.set_ylim(0, 115)
    ax.set_yticks(range(0, 101, 20))
    ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, frameon=False)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax.set_ylabel("Survival rate (%)")

flags = train.assign(AgeKnown=train["Age"].notna(), CabinKnown=train["Cabin"].notna())

Figure 3. Survival rate by whether age and cabin were recorded. Use the tabs to switch between the two. The dashed line is the overall survival rate, and numbers in brackets are group sizes.

Passengers with no recorded age survived 29.4% of the time compared with 40.6% for those with a recorded age, and passengers with no recorded cabin survived 30.0% compared with 66.7% for those with a cabin. The data are therefore not missing completely at random, and it is worth keeping simple “was it recorded?” flags next to the imputed values. Cabin in particular tells us more through whether it exists than through its content, so we do not try to fill it in.

Decisions for missing data. We fill in age using the median age of passengers with the same title, because titles such as “Master” (boys) and “Mrs” separate age groups far better than one overall median. We fill the missing ports with the most common port, and the single missing fare in the test file with the median fare of the same ticket class. For cabin we keep only a yes/no flag. All fill-in values are learned from the training data only and then applied unchanged to the test data, so no information leaks from the test file.

2.5 Comparing each feature with survival

We now look at each feature on its own against survival. Throughout, the dashed line in the bar charts marks the overall survival rate of 38%.

Code 
def extract_title(names):
    """Pull the title (Mr, Mrs, ...) out of a passenger name and group the rare ones."""
    t = names.str.extract(r" ([A-Za-z]+)\.", expand=False)
    t = t.replace({"Mlle": "Miss", "Ms": "Miss", "Mme": "Mrs"})
    return t.where(t.isin(["Mr", "Mrs", "Miss", "Master"]), "Rare")

def add_simple_features(df):
    """Features that need no learned values, so they are safe to build on any dataset."""
    out = df.copy()
    out["Title"] = extract_title(out["Name"])
    out["FamilySize"] = out["SibSp"] + out["Parch"] + 1
    out["IsAlone"] = (out["FamilySize"] == 1).astype(int)
    out["HasCabin"] = out["Cabin"].notna().astype(int)
    out["AgeMissing"] = out["Age"].isna().astype(int)
    return out

eda = add_simple_features(eda)

Figure 4. Survival rate by sex, by passenger class and by both together. Use the tabs to switch between the three views.

Sex is the strongest single signal in the data. In the training data 74.2% of women survived compared with 18.9% of men (Figure 4, Sex tab). Survival also falls steadily with passenger class, from 63.0% in first class to 47.3% in second and 24.2% in third (Figure 4, Passenger class tab). Both patterns match historical accounts of the sinking, where women were prioritised for lifeboats and survival declined with social class (Hall 1986; Elinder and Erixson 2012).

The third tab, “Sex and class together”, shows that the two effects combine. Almost all women in first class (96.8%) and second class (92.1%) survived, but only half of the women in third class (50.0%). Men in every class did poorly, from 36.9% in first class down to 13.5% in third. This is an interaction: the effect of class depends on sex. A model that can capture interactions, or that includes both features, should do much better than one that uses either alone.

Include in the model? Yes, both sex and passenger class.

Figure 5. Age distribution of survivors and non-survivors, and survival rate by age group. Use the tabs to switch views. Only passengers with a recorded age are shown.

The age distributions of survivors and non-survivors overlap heavily, but survivors have a clear extra bump of very young children (Figure 5, Age distribution tab). By group, 58.0% of children aged 12 or under survived, compared with 38.3% of passengers aged 19 to 35 and only 22.7% of those aged 61 or over (Figure 5, Survival by age group tab). The survival rate is nearly flat from age 19 to 60 (38.3% and 40.0%), so the age effect is concentrated in the youngest and oldest groups, which are small (69 and 22 passengers). A pattern like this shows up only weakly in a single correlation number.

Include in the model? Age is a weak feature overall, so it will not be among our top-correlated features, but the child effect in Figure 5 is real. We keep age in the processed data as an optional feature to test in flexible models. It needs imputation for the 19.9% of passengers with no age.

Figure 6. Distribution of the log fare for survivors and non-survivors, and the log fare within each passenger class. Use the tabs to switch views.

Fares are extremely right-skewed (skewness of about 4.8), with a maximum of 512.33 pounds and 15 passengers who paid nothing, so we work with the logarithm of one plus the fare instead of the raw value. Survivors paid more: the median fare was 26.0 pounds for survivors and 10.5 pounds for non-survivors. Part of that is simply passenger class, because fare and class are strongly linked, but within first and second class the survivors still paid somewhat more, while in third class the two groups paid almost the same (Figure 6, Fare within each class tab).

Include in the model? Yes, in its log form. It overlaps with passenger class, which we take into account in the feature selection below.

Figure 7. Survival rate by family size and by whether the passenger travelled alone. Use the tabs to switch views.

We combined the number of siblings or spouses and the number of parents or children into a single family size (the passenger plus these relatives). Survival is not a straight-line function of family size. People travelling alone survived 30.4% of the time, small families of two to four did best (55.3%, 57.8% and 72.4%), and large families of five or more did worst, with only 16.1% surviving (Figure 7, Family size tab). Collapsing this into “alone versus with family” keeps the main contrast, 30.4% versus 50.6% (Figure 7, Travelling alone tab), in a single clean feature.

Include in the model? We keep the “travelling alone” indicator. The separate counts of siblings and spouses and of parents and children have almost no linear relationship with survival (shown below), and family size is almost the same information as the alone flag.

Figure 8. Survival rate by port of boarding and the mix of passenger classes among passengers boarding at each port. Use the tabs to switch views. Two passengers with no recorded port are left out.

Passengers who boarded at Cherbourg survived more often (55.4%) than those from Queenstown (39.0%) or Southampton (33.7%). The “Class mix by port” tab offers a likely reason: 50.6% of the Cherbourg passengers travelled first class, against 19.7% at Southampton. The port effect is therefore partly the class effect in disguise, although Cherbourg passengers in third class still fared better than those from Southampton (37.9% versus 19.0%).

Include in the model? It is a weak, partly redundant signal, so it is a lower-priority feature. We keep it as an indicator for Cherbourg and let the ranking below decide whether it makes our top five.

Figure 9. Survival rate by title, and by passenger class and whether a cabin was recorded. Use the tabs to switch views.

Titles pack sex, age and marital status into one feature: “Master” (young boys) survived 57.5% of the time, while men titled “Mr” survived only 15.7%, and “Miss” and “Mrs” survived 70.3% and 79.4%. This is mostly the sex effect again, with the useful extra detail that boys fared far better than men.

Having a cabin recorded is linked to survival in every class (Figure 9, Cabin tab), although only 16 second-class and 12 third-class passengers have one, so those bars are noisy. A possible explanation is that cabin numbers were more likely to be recorded for people who survived to be interviewed, but these data cannot test that. Because most cabin information is missing and a recorded cabin is closely tied to first class, we treat it with care.

Include in the model? Title overlaps almost completely with sex, so we keep it in the processed data for later experiments but do not select it. The cabin-recorded flag is kept only if it adds something beyond passenger class, which we test in the correlation analysis.

2.5.7 Columns we exclude

The passenger identifier is only a row number and cannot help predict survival. The name is used only to extract the title. The ticket number is a mix of codes with many unique values; a possible future feature is the number of passengers sharing a ticket, but we leave that out for now to keep the analysis simple.

2.6 Transforming the data for modelling

We now turn the cleaned columns into a form a model can use. The steps are: fill in the missing values using statistics learned from the training data only, create the extra features described above, take the logarithm of the fare, and convert categories to 0/1 columns. We deliberately do not scale the numeric columns here. Scaling will be done inside the modelling pipeline, so that its mean and spread are also learned from training data only.

Code

fill_values = {
    "age_by_title": train_feat.groupby("Title")["Age"].median(),
    "age_overall": train_feat["Age"].median(),
    "embarked_mode": train_feat["Embarked"].mode()[0],
    "fare_by_class": train_feat.groupby("Pclass")["Fare"].median(),
    "fare_overall": train_feat["Fare"].median(),
}

Code 
TITLES = ["Master", "Miss", "Mr", "Mrs", "Rare"]

def preprocess(df, fv):
    """Impute, engineer and encode features using fill values learned from the training set."""
    out = add_simple_features(df)
    out["Age"] = out["Age"].fillna(out["Title"].map(fv["age_by_title"])).fillna(fv["age_overall"])
    out["Embarked"] = out["Embarked"].fillna(fv["embarked_mode"])
    out["Fare"] = out["Fare"].fillna(out["Pclass"].map(fv["fare_by_class"])).fillna(fv["fare_overall"])
    out["FareLog"] = np.log1p(out["Fare"])
    out["Sex_female"] = (out["Sex"] == "female").astype(int)
    for port in ["C", "Q", "S"]:
        out[f"Embarked_{port}"] = (out["Embarked"] == port).astype(int)
    for t in TITLES:
        out[f"Title_{t}"] = (out["Title"] == t).astype(int)
    return out

FEATURES = [
    "Pclass", "Sex_female", "Age", "SibSp", "Parch", "Fare", "FareLog", "FamilySize",
    "IsAlone", "HasCabin", "AgeMissing", "Embarked_C", "Embarked_Q", "Embarked_S",
] + [f"Title_{t}" for t in TITLES]

train_p = preprocess(train, fill_values)
test_p = preprocess(test, fill_values)

# Every modelling column must now be complete in all three datasets.
for name, d in [("training", train_p), ("test", test_p)]:
    assert d[FEATURES].isna().sum().sum() == 0, f"missing values left in {name} data"
print("No missing values remain in any modelling column.")
train_p[FEATURES].dtypes.value_counts().rename("Number of columns").to_frame()
No missing values remain in any modelling column.

Table 5. Data types of the modelling columns after the transformations. All 19 columns are numeric.

All 19 candidate modelling columns are now numeric and complete in both the training and the test data.

2.7 Which features relate most strongly to survival?

We now measure the relationship between every feature and survival, and between the features themselves. We use the Pearson correlation coefficient, which for 0/1 columns is also known as the point-biserial or phi coefficient. It runs from -1 to 1: a positive value means the feature goes up when survival is more likely, and a negative value means the opposite. We compute it on the imputed training set, so the correlation for age includes the filled-in ages.

2.7.1 Correlation matrix

Code 
LABELS = {
    "Survived": "Survived", "Pclass": "Passenger class", "Sex_female": "Female", "Age": "Age",
    "SibSp": "Siblings/spouses", "Parch": "Parents/children", "FareLog": "Fare (log)",
    "FamilySize": "Family size", "IsAlone": "Travelling alone", "HasCabin": "Cabin recorded",
    "AgeMissing": "Age missing", "Embarked_C": "Boarded Cherbourg", "Embarked_Q": "Boarded Queenstown",
    "Embarked_S": "Boarded Southampton", "Title_Master": "Title: Master", "Title_Miss": "Title: Miss",
    "Title_Mr": "Title: Mr", "Title_Mrs": "Title: Mrs", "Title_Rare": "Title: Rare",
}
heat_cols = list(LABELS)
corr = train_p[["Survived"] + FEATURES].corr()
heat = corr.loc[heat_cols, heat_cols]
mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(heat, dtype=bool), k=1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.5, 8.3))
sns.heatmap(heat, mask=mask, annot=True, fmt=".2f", annot_kws={"size": 7.5},
            cmap="RdBu_r", center=0, vmin=-1, vmax=1, linewidths=0.4, linecolor="white",
            xticklabels=[LABELS[c] for c in heat_cols], yticklabels=[LABELS[c] for c in heat_cols],
            cbar_kws={"label": "Pearson correlation", "shrink": 0.8}, ax=ax)
plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha="right")
plt.yticks(rotation=0)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Figure 10. Correlation matrix of survival and the candidate features in the training set. Red means a positive correlation and blue a negative one. Fare is shown on the log scale.

The first column of the heatmap shows how each feature relates to survival, and the rest shows how the features relate to each other. Three things stand out.

First, the strongest links with survival are being female (0.54), having the title “Mr” (-0.55), travelling in a lower class, meaning a higher class number (-0.34), and the log fare (0.33). Second, several features are close to duplicates of each other. Being female and having the title “Mr” are almost mirror images (-0.87), boarding at Cherbourg and at Southampton are nearly opposite (-0.78), a recorded cabin follows passenger class (-0.73), and family size follows the alone flag (-0.69). Third, passenger class and the log fare are also related (-0.66), so they partly carry the same information.

2.7.2 Ranking the features

Correlation only picks up straight-line relationships, so we also compute the mutual information between each feature and survival, which can detect any kind of dependence. It acts as a second opinion, particularly for age, where the effect is not linear.

Code 
corr_target = corr["Survived"].drop("Survived")

# Pick the top features by absolute correlation, skipping any that are nearly duplicates
# (|r| >= 0.70) of one we already picked. We rank one representative per idea:
# the title columns (which mostly repeat sex) and raw fare (replaced by log fare) are left out.
CANDIDATES = ["Sex_female", "Pclass", "HasCabin", "FareLog", "IsAlone", "Embarked_C",
              "Age", "Parch", "FamilySize", "SibSp", "AgeMissing"]
K, REDUNDANT_AT = 5, 0.70
selected, rows = [], []
for f in corr_target[CANDIDATES].abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index:
    clash = [(s, corr.loc[f, s]) for s in selected if abs(corr.loc[f, s]) >= REDUNDANT_AT]
    if len(selected) >= K:
        decision, reason = "Not selected", "top five already chosen"
    elif clash:
        decision, reason = "Not selected", f"near-duplicate of {LABELS[clash[0][0]].lower()} (r = {clash[0][1]:.2f})"
    else:
        selected.append(f)
        decision, reason = "Selected", "high correlation, not redundant"
    rows.append([LABELS[f], round(corr_target[f], 3), decision, reason])
selection = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Feature", "Correlation with survival", "Decision", "Reason"])

mi = pd.Series(
    mutual_info_classif(train_p[FEATURES], train_p["Survived"], random_state=SEED,
                        discrete_features=[f not in ("Age", "Fare", "FareLog") for f in FEATURES]),
    index=FEATURES,
).sort_values(ascending=False)
order = corr_target.abs().sort_values().index
mi_order = mi.sort_values()

Table 6. Selection of the five features most strongly correlated with survival, skipping near-duplicates of features already chosen.

The five features we select are sex, passenger class, log fare, travelling alone and boarding at Cherbourg. They come from walking down the correlation ranking and skipping any feature that nearly repeats one already chosen. The “cabin recorded” flag has the fourth-highest correlation (0.32) but is skipped because it is almost the same as passenger class (-0.73), and most of its values are missing in the first place. The title columns are left out of the ranking because they mostly restate sex (-0.87 with the title “Mr”), even though their raw correlations are as high as the top feature. The raw fare is replaced by the log fare, which correlates better with survival (0.33 versus 0.26).

Two caveats matter. The log fare is just below our 0.70 cut-off for redundancy with passenger class (-0.66), so these two overlap noticeably, and the modelling stage should check that fare adds something beyond class. And boarding at Cherbourg is the weakest of the five (0.17) and partly reflects class, as seen in Figure 8.

The mutual information ranking agrees that sex, title and fare are the most informative. It scores travelling alone (0.021) and boarding at Cherbourg (0.014) much lower, which is another reason to treat those two as weak features. Age scores low as well (0.016), matching its weak correlation (-0.08), so the child effect we saw in Figure 5 is too concentrated in a small group to stand out in these overall measures. Family size is the opposite case: its correlation with survival is close to zero (0.02), yet its mutual information (0.048) is higher than that of travelling alone, which fits the non-straight-line pattern in Figure 7. We keep age and family size in the processed data as optional extras for flexible models, but they are not among the five features selected by correlation.

2.8 Summary of the exploratory analysis

Feature Decision Main reason
Sex Include Strongest single signal (see Figure 4).
Passenger class Include Survival falls steadily from first to third class and interacts with sex.
Fare (log) Include Survivors paid more; the log scale removes the extreme skew. Overlaps with class.
Travelling alone Include People travelling alone survived much less often than those with family.
Port: Cherbourg Include (weak) Higher survival, but mostly a first-class effect.
Age Optional Weak by both measures, but children survived more; needs imputation.
Title Optional Mostly repeats sex; adds boys versus men.
Cabin recorded Drop Nearly the same as passenger class; mostly missing.
Siblings/spouses, parents/children Drop Almost no link with survival; the alone flag keeps the useful part.
Family size Optional No linear link, but a non-linear pattern; the alone flag is the simpler version.
Passenger ID, name, ticket Drop Identifiers, or only useful through the title.

Table 7. Summary of our decision for each feature.

In short, a passenger’s chance of survival depended most on being a woman, travelling in a higher class and having paid a higher fare, with smaller contributions from travelling with family and from the port of boarding. About a fifth of the ages and most of the cabins were missing, and the missing values were themselves linked to survival. These findings describe associations in this one historical dataset; they do not show that any single factor caused a passenger to survive.

Two limitations apply to the conclusions above. First, correlation and mutual information look at one feature at a time, so they can miss combinations such as the sex-by-class interaction in Figure 4, and a feature that is weak on its own may still help a model. Second, our training data contains only 891 passengers, so small groups (for example older passengers or the rare titles) give noisy rates, and our selected features should be treated as a starting point that the model comparison can confirm or revise.

2.9 Saving the processed data

We save the processed training and test data to the processed data folder, both using the fill values learned from the training data. The files keep all 19 candidate features, so the modelling stage can choose among them, together with the passenger identifier and, for the training file, the survival outcome. Our five selected features are stored in a short text file so that teammates can load the same list.

3 Predictive modelling with logistic regression

In this section, we build a classification pipeline using LogisticRegression (Pedregosa et al. 2011) wrapped with StandardScaler inside a scikit-learn Pipeline. Applying standardization inside the pipeline ensures that feature means and standard deviations are learned strictly within each training fold during 5-fold stratified cross-validation (SEED = 522).

To connect our EDA findings with the modelling stage without repeating the individual feature analyses, we test whether adding the optional features kept in data/processed/ (Age, FamilySize, and passenger title indicators Title_Master, Title_Miss, Title_Mrs) together with the Sex_female × Pclass interaction identified in Figure 4 improves cross-validation performance over the five correlation-selected features (selected_features.txt).

Code 
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_validate, cross_val_predict
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, confusion_matrix, roc_curve

train_mod = pd.read_csv(PROC_DIR / "train_processed.csv")
test_mod = pd.read_csv(PROC_DIR / "test_processed.csv")
selected_5 = (PROC_DIR / "selected_features.txt").read_text().strip().splitlines()

for df_m in (train_mod, test_mod):
    df_m["Sex_x_Pclass"] = df_m["Sex_female"] * df_m["Pclass"]

extended_cols = selected_5 + [
    "Age", "FamilySize", "Sex_x_Pclass", "Title_Master", "Title_Miss", "Title_Mrs"
]
y_train = train_mod["Survived"]
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
scoring = ["accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1", "roc_auc"]

dummy_res = cross_validate(
    DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"),
    train_mod[selected_5], y_train, cv=cv, scoring=["accuracy", "roc_auc"]
)
cv_rows = [{
    "Model": "Baseline (DummyClassifier: most frequent)",
    "Features (p)": len(selected_5),
    "CV Accuracy (mean ± SD)": f"{dummy_res['test_accuracy'].mean():.3f} ± {dummy_res['test_accuracy'].std():.3f}",
    "Precision": 0.0,
    "Recall": 0.0,
    "F1-score": 0.0,
    "ROC-AUC": dummy_res["test_roc_auc"].mean(),
}]

for label, cols in [
    ("Logistic regression (5 selected features)", selected_5),
    ("Logistic regression (5 selected + optional & interaction)", extended_cols),
]:
    pipe = Pipeline([
        ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
        ("logreg", LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=1000, random_state=SEED)),
    ])
    res = cross_validate(pipe, train_mod[cols], y_train, cv=cv, scoring=scoring)
    cv_rows.append({
        "Model": label,
        "Features (p)": len(cols),
        "CV Accuracy (mean ± SD)": f"{res['test_accuracy'].mean():.3f} ± {res['test_accuracy'].std():.3f}",
        "Precision": res["test_precision"].mean(),
        "Recall": res["test_recall"].mean(),
        "F1-score": res["test_f1"].mean(),
        "ROC-AUC": res["test_roc_auc"].mean(),
    })

display(pd.DataFrame(cv_rows).round(3))

Table 8. Five-fold stratified cross-validation performance comparing the majority-class baseline, logistic regression on the 5 correlation-selected features, and logistic regression adding the optional features and Sex × Pclass interaction.

Table 8 shows that logistic regression on the five correlation-selected features (Sex_female, Pclass, FareLog, IsAlone, Embarked_C) achieves 77.4% cross-validation accuracy (ROC-AUC = 0.835), beating the 61.6% majority-class baseline by 15.8 percentage points. Adding the optional features (Age, FamilySize, and title indicators) and the Sex_female × Pclass interaction further lifts cross-validation accuracy by 5.2 percentage points to 82.6% (F1 = 0.761, ROC-AUC = 0.871), confirming that controlling for age, family size, youth/marital titles, and the sex-by-class interaction adds substantial predictive power in a multivariable linear model.

We inspect out-of-fold predictions and standardized coefficients for the extended logistic regression model across the 891 training passengers, and save the resulting predictions for the 418 unlabelled test passengers to data/processed/test_predictions.csv.

Across all 891 training passengers, the model correctly classifies 88.9% of non-survivors (490/549) and 71.9% of survivors (246/342), with a precision of 80.7% (Figure 12). On the 418 unlabelled test passengers, it predicts 160 survivors (38.3%), matching the 38.4% observed training survival rate.

4 Discussion and conclusions

Our results show that a regularized logistic regression pipeline predicts Titanic passenger survival with 77.4% 5-fold cross-validation accuracy using the five correlation-selected features (Sex_female, Pclass, FareLog, IsAlone, Embarked_C), well above the 61.6% majority-class baseline. Incorporating the optional features identified during our EDA (Age, FamilySize, and passenger titles) together with the Sex_female × Pclass interaction lifts cross-validation accuracy to 82.6% (F1 = 0.761, ROC-AUC = 0.871). The standardized weights confirm that passenger sex, youth and marital titles (Title_Master, Title_Mrs, Title_Miss), ticket class, log fare, and family size are the primary predictors, consistent with historical accounts of the evacuation (Hall 1986; Elinder and Erixson 2012).

Two main limitations apply to this baseline analysis: (1) our findings describe statistical associations in a single 1912 dataset rather than causal effects, and missing values in Age (20%) and Cabin (77%) were not missing completely at random; and (2) we evaluated default \(L_2\) regularization (\(C = 1.0\)) with a linear log-odds boundary, where recall on survivors (71.9%) remains lower than specificity on non-survivors (88.9%). Future work can explore hyperparameter tuning of the regularization strength \(C\), probability threshold adjustment, or non-linear classifiers.
